cell_context_text: Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal neurons (especially pyramidal and glutamatergic neurons) and their synaptic terminals, where APP and receptor internalization shape Aβ production and synaptic plasticity.
Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons, where high secretory load for APP, synaptic receptors, and neuropeptides make ER-lumen stress particularly damaging.

Central in pre- and postsynaptic neuronal compartments across hippocampus and association cortex, and also in microglia and astrocytes where vesicular trafficking governs cytokine release and phagocytic processing of Aβ.
Prominent in neurons and astrocytes of AD-affected regions (hippocampus, entorhinal cortex), where disturbed Ca²⁺ handling and ER stress responses are well documented.

The most relevant context is vulnerable neurons in hippocampus and association cortex, where stress from Aβ, tau, excitotoxicity, and metabolic compromise culminates in apoptotic signaling; glial cells (astrocytes, microglia) may also engage apoptosis in chronic neuroinflammation but the key disease-defining impact is neuronal loss in these regions.
Especially pertinent to neurons in cortex and hippocampus, where early endosomal enlargement is observed, but also to microglia handling Aβ uptake.

Particularly pertinent to excitatory synapses in hippocampal and cortical neurons, as well as neuron–glia contact sites at tripartite synapses and along myelinated axons, where adhesion dynamics influence synapse stability and circuit connectivity in AD.
Highly relevant in presynaptic terminals and dendrites of excitatory neurons in hippocampus and association cortex, where neurotransmitter and neurotrophin vesicle cycling is critical.
Central in neurons and microglia within plaque-rich cortical and hippocampal areas, where defective lysosomal clearance contributes to dystrophic neurites and intracellular Aβ/tau accumulation.

Most relevant in excitatory pyramidal neurons and hippocampal/cortical synapses, where Ca2+-dependent signaling governs neurotransmitter release and plasticity, and in vulnerable neuronal populations exposed to Aβ-induced Ca2+ dysregulation in AD.

Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons, where APP and tau are heavily processed and where secretory/Golgi dysfunction directly impacts synaptic receptor trafficking; supporting roles are also likely in astrocytes and microglia, which rely on glycosylation for receptor and cytokine handling but are secondary to the neuronal context for this module.
Most relevant in neurons and glia (particularly microglia), where lysosomal overload and defective autophagy drive neuritic plaques and impaired Aβ/tau clearance.
Most relevant to neurons (particularly cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons) and their synapses, where Ca²⁺-binding proteins regulate neurotransmitter release, excitability, and plasticity.
Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons and their synapses, where APP and neurotransmitter receptors undergo intense endocytic cycling.
Particularly important in neurons and astrocytes controlling surface levels of LDLR/LRP1 and INSR, thereby modulating Aβ clearance and metabolic signaling.
Critical in excitatory cortical and hippocampal neurons, where receptor and APP endocytosis directly shape synaptic plasticity and Aβ generation.
Acts across neurons, astrocytes, and brain endothelial cells that orchestrate uptake of lipoproteins, APP, and growth factor receptors.
Most relevant in neurons under chronic proteotoxic stress, but also in astrocytes and microglia managing high secretory loads of inflammatory mediators and apolipoproteins.
Forebrain glutamatergic synapses in cortex and hippocampus, which show early dysfunction and structural loss in AD.
Neuronal and astrocytic ER, especially in large projection neurons vulnerable to proteostatic stress.
Pyramidal neurons and other projection neurons where high secretory load and Ca²⁺ flux make ER stress particularly damaging in AD.
Brain interstitial fluid and perivascular spaces, where Aβ accumulates, diffuses, and is cleared, as well as vascular interfaces relevant to cerebral amyloid angiopathy.
Neuronal Golgi in cortical and hippocampal neurons, which undergo fragmentation and trafficking alterations in AD.
Neuron-, microglia-, and astrocyte-derived exosomes in brain parenchyma and CSF, serving as vehicles of Aβ and tau spread and as potential biomarkers.

Highly relevant to astrocytes (primary CNS cholesterol producers), microglia (lipid sensing and efflux), and neurons (cholesterol uptake and membrane remodeling), as well as brain endothelium at the BBB.
Central to astrocytes (primary cholesterol producers in brain) and neurons (cholesterol consumers) in cortex and hippocampus, especially in APOE-expressing glia and LDLR/LRP1-expressing neurons.
Similar context to cholesterol homeostasis, spanning astrocyte–neuron lipid exchange and possibly microglia responding to lipid-rich debris and plaques.

Reflects widespread neuronal and glial protein-interaction networks, but is especially pertinent at synapses and endosomal compartments where multi-protein complexes mediate signaling and trafficking in AD.
Predominantly active in microglia and astrocytes within the CNS parenchyma, with contributions from endothelial and peripheral immune cells at the neurovascular interface.
Most prominent in long-projecting neurons requiring efficient axonal and dendritic vesicle trafficking, including synaptic vesicle recycling and receptor transport.
Most relevant in neurons, astrocytes, and brain endothelial cells, where LRP1 and SORL1 regulate APP and Aβ trafficking and lipoprotein uptake.
Pertinent to astrocytes and neurons that exchange triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, influencing brain lipid distribution and APOE-related AD risk.

Central at neuronal synapses, perivascular regions, and glial surfaces (astrocytes, microglia), where PRNP, CLU, and LRP1 interact with extracellular Aβ and shape plaque formation and synaptotoxic signaling.

pathway_name: low-density lipoprotein particle receptor catabolic process
cell_context_text: Key in astrocytes, neurons, and brain endothelial cells that internalize apoE-containing lipoproteins and participate in Aβ clearance at the BBB and within the parenchyma.

pathway_name: regulation of low-density lipoprotein particle receptor catabolic process
cell_context_text: Operates in the same cell types, fine-tuning receptor abundance and thus the capacity for lipid uptake and Aβ handling.

Most relevant in stressed cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons and also in chronically activated glial cells (astrocytes and microglia) in AD brains, where high loads of misfolded APP, Aβ, and tau trigger sustained ER stress.

Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons, where high secretory demand for synaptic proteins and APP makes ER-membrane proteostasis crucial; astrocytes and microglia also contribute via secretory inflammatory mediators but likely with a secondary role for this particular module.

Similarly most pertinent in excitatory neurons of vulnerable brain regions (entorhinal cortex, hippocampus, association cortex), where chronic ER stress, calcium dysregulation, and aberrant APP processing converge; the validated ER-localized gene set likely shapes neuronal resilience versus degeneration in these tissues.

Most relevant in neurons and astrocytes of cortex and hippocampus, where cholesterol synthesis, export, and membrane remodeling directly influence synaptic integrity, APP processing, and plaque formation; microglia are also implicated via lipid handling and phagocytosis of Aβ.

Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal neurons and plaque-associated glia (especially microglia and astrocytes), where lipid-binding proteins regulate synaptic membrane composition, APP/secretase localization in lipid rafts, and glial lipid storage and remodeling around amyloid plaques.
Most relevant to pyramidal neurons in hippocampus and association cortex, and to vulnerable basal forebrain cholinergic neurons undergoing programmed cell death in AD.
Most relevant to cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons in human brain, where APP processing, tau pathology, and synaptic/mitochondrial dysfunction converge.
Primarily hippocampal and cortical neurons receiving BDNF/NGF support, but also relevant to basal forebrain cholinergic neurons that degenerate in AD.
Neurons and astrocytes of cortex and hippocampus, where autophagic vacuoles and dystrophic neurites accumulate; also microglia involved in clearance of aggregates.

Highly pertinent to neurons within hippocampal and cortical circuits where JNK/ERK signaling modulates tau phosphorylation and synaptic plasticity, with additional roles in activated microglia and astrocytes.

Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons, where cytosolic tau aggregation, ubiquitin–p62-positive inclusions, and proteostasis collapse are prominent in AD, but also in activated microglia/astrocytes managing proteotoxic stress.
Applies to cortical and hippocampal projection neurons and their axons/terminals, where altered guidance cue signaling can drive synapse loss and network remodeling.

Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons undergoing chronic proteotoxic stress in AD, but also in astrocytes and microglia where altered ubiquitination modulates inflammatory signaling and clearance of protein aggregates.
Most relevant to vulnerable cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons undergoing programmed cell death in AD, with contributions from stressed glia at later stages.
Operative in neurons and glial cells in cortex and hippocampus, where dynamic tuning of death thresholds determines selective vulnerability and survival.
Neurons (especially in hippocampus and association cortex) showing ubiquitin-positive inclusions, as well as glial cells participating in turnover of damaged proteins and synaptic elements.
Particularly important in neurons that are chronically stressed yet temporarily maintained, and in microglia/astrocytes where anti-apoptotic signaling shapes neuroinflammatory responses.

pathway_name: Regulation of TP53 Activity through Phosphorylation
cell_context_text: Most relevant in stressed neurons and glial cells in AD-affected regions, where DNA damage and oxidative stress trigger p53 activation.
Central to neuronal soma and synaptic terminals in hippocampus and cortex, as well as in astrocytes, where efficient mitochondrial turnover is critical for high metabolic demands.
Most relevant to neurons in late-stage plaques-and-tangles regions (e.g., hippocampus, association cortex) where pro-death signaling predominates, leading to overt cell loss.

Especially pertinent to long-projection neurons in hippocampus and association cortex, where microtubule destabilization and axonal transport failure precede neuron loss, and to dendritic spines in these regions where cytoskeletal remodeling underlies synaptic dysfunction.
Broadly relevant across neurons and glia in gray matter regions with heavy plaque/tangle burden, governing bulk clearance of protein aggregates and organelles.
Reflects pan-neuronal and glial lysosomal-autophagic activity throughout AD-vulnerable brain areas, including hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, and association cortices.

Most relevant in neurons and astrocytes within vulnerable cortical and hippocampal regions, where energy metabolism deficits and dysregulated autophagy are prominent, but also in microglia where AMPK influences inflammatory responses and phagocytic capacity in the AD brain.
Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons and associated glia, where survival and insulin/IGF signaling modulate vulnerability to Aβ and tau.
Most relevant to cortical and hippocampal glutamatergic pyramidal neurons and their long-range projections, as well as to local circuit interneurons undergoing synaptic remodeling in AD.
Active in neurons and glial cells in hippocampus and association cortex, mediating stress, inflammatory, and tau-phosphorylating responses.

Most relevant to cortical and hippocampal neurons, particularly excitatory pyramidal cells where endosomal APP processing and receptor trafficking occur, with important contributions from microglia and astrocytes in receptor and debris uptake.
Most relevant to excitatory glutamatergic synapses in hippocampal and cortical pyramidal neurons, which are heavily affected in AD.
Most relevant in excitatory neurons and their synapses, particularly cortical and hippocampal pyramidal cells where adhesion molecules organize spines and synaptic contacts vulnerable in AD.

Broadly relevant in neurons and glia, with critical impact in energy-demanding hippocampal and cortical neurons where ATP-dependent kinases, motors, and pumps maintain signaling and structural integrity.
Primarily engages developing and remodeling neurons in hippocampus and association cortex, where dendritic spine dynamics and axonal projections underlie memory circuits vulnerable in AD.

pathway_name: positive regulation of neuron projection development
cell_context_text: Contextualized in hippocampal and cortical neurons undergoing activity-dependent structural plasticity, including compensatory sprouting or attempts at circuit repair in prodromal and early AD.
Specifically implicates cortical and hippocampal excitatory circuits mediating learning and memory.
Pertains to long-range corticocortical and cortico-hippocampal axons and apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons.
Maps to pre- and postsynaptic membranes of cortical and hippocampal neurons where Aβ interacts with receptors.

Central to synapses of hippocampal and cortical neurons (both glutamatergic and GABAergic), as well as key neuromodulatory inputs from basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, all of which are perturbed in AD.

Particularly important in neurons (axons, dendritic spines) and microglia, where small GTPases control vesicle trafficking, process motility, and receptor endocytosis central to amyloid handling and synaptic dynamics.
Most relevant to dendritic spines of hippocampal CA1 and cortical layer II/III neurons showing early PSD disorganization.
Best mapped to hippocampal CA1–CA3 and entorhinal circuits where LTP/LTD and memory encoding occur and show early impairment in AD.
Relevant across neurons and glial cells (astrocytes, microglia) in cortex and hippocampus, where GPCRs mediate neuromodulation, neuroinflammation, and vascular responses in AD.
Localized to spines on hippocampal and cortical pyramidal neuron dendrites undergoing retraction in early AD.

Highly relevant in neurons of the hippocampus and association cortex, where kinases regulate tau phosphorylation and synaptic plasticity pathways; also relevant in glia modulating inflammatory signaling.

pathway_name: negative regulation of neuron projection development
cell_context_text: Likely localized to cortical and hippocampal neurons undergoing progressive neuritic retraction and spine loss near amyloid plaques and in tau-affected regions.
Key in hippocampal and cortical synapses where altered receptor trafficking and signaling drive cognitive deficits.
Reflects soma in hippocampal, cortical, and basal forebrain cholinergic neurons that exhibit atrophy and inclusion pathology.
Most relevant in presynaptic and postsynaptic compartments of neurons, where GTPase effectors orchestrate vesicle fusion, spine morphology, and receptor trafficking.
Particularly pertinent to long-lived cortical and hippocampal neurons where autophagic flux is critical for clearing aggregated proteins and damaged organelles.
Acts in neurons and glial cells throughout affected brain regions; neuronal autophagy in hippocampus and cortex is particularly pertinent for clearance of misfolded proteins in AD.
Critical in neurons of AD-vulnerable regions (entorhinal cortex, hippocampus) where phosphatases like PP2A regulate tau phosphorylation and synaptic signaling thresholds.

pathway_name: positive regulation of cytosolic calcium ion concentration
cell_context_text: Most relevant in hippocampal and cortical neurons where Ca²⁺ signaling couples synaptic activity to plasticity and where pathological Ca²⁺ elevations drive excitotoxicity in AD.
Broadly relevant to neuronal and glial cell surfaces in AD cortex and hippocampus where extracellular aggregates signal.
Applies to neurons (dendritic spines and survival signaling), astrocytes, and vascular cells where RTK–PI3K–AKT supports trophic responses and barrier integrity.
Primarily neuronal (synaptic plasticity, memory circuits in hippocampus and cortex) and glial (microglia/astrocyte stress and inflammatory responses) in the AD brain.
Centered on neurons, especially dendritic spines of cortical and hippocampal neurons where RAC1-dependent actin remodeling governs spine structure, but also relevant to glial motility and morphology.
Most relevant to cerebrovascular cells, particularly pericytes and smooth muscle cells at the neurovascular unit, with secondary roles in astrocytes and microglia responding to PDGF cues.
Central in hippocampal and cortical excitatory neurons that rely on BDNF–TrkB for synaptic plasticity and memory formation.
Key in excitatory synapses of hippocampus and neocortex, where Ca2+ influx through voltage-gated channels and downstream CAMK2A/B signaling underlies LTP/LTD and is perturbed in AD.
Applies to glutamatergic presynaptic terminals in hippocampus and cortex exhibiting impaired release in AD models.
Represents presynaptic terminals across these brain regions, with particular relevance to hippocampal Schaffer collateral and perforant path synapses.

pathway_name: regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II
cell_context_text: Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons and associated glia, where widespread transcriptional reprogramming occurs during AD progression.

The most relevant contexts are neurons and microglia in the hippocampus and cortex, where dynamic assembly of transcriptional and chromatin complexes in response to activity, Aβ, and inflammatory cues dictates synaptic plasticity, stress resilience, and neuroinflammatory tone in AD.

Particularly pertinent to neurons in memory-critical regions (e.g., hippocampus) and perhaps microglia/astrocytes, where altered mRNA processing and stability affect synaptic, inflammatory, and stress-response gene expression.
Predominantly neuronal plasma membranes in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons, where APP, glutamate receptors, and adhesion molecules reside.
Neuronal cytoplasm in soma and neurites, where trafficking and degradation machinery assemblies operate in AD-affected brain regions.
Neuronal synaptic junctions and possibly neuron–glia contacts in gray matter regions vulnerable in AD.
Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons and their synapses, where APP and glutamate receptor internalization are tightly regulated and heavily implicated in early AD changes.

Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons, particularly at pre- and postsynaptic specializations and perisynaptic astrocyte contacts where adhesion molecules stabilize synapses and organize signaling complexes vulnerable in AD.
Excitatory synapses of hippocampal and cortical pyramidal neurons, key sites of early synaptic dysfunction in AD.

Most relevant to cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons in AD, where high secretory load (APP, synaptic proteins) and chronic stress drive ER overload, but also to reactive glia (astrocytes and microglia) that upregulate ER chaperones during neuroinflammatory responses.
Broadly, synapses in hippocampus and association cortex undergoing degenerative changes in AD.
Neuronal Golgi stacks in soma and dendrites, including Golgi outposts involved in local protein processing in AD-vulnerable neurons.
Neuronal and neuritic lysosomes and autolysosomes in cortical and hippocampal neurons, as well as within dystrophic neurites surrounding plaques.
Operative in neurons and glia across the secretory and endosomal pathways, particularly in hippocampal and association cortices where trafficking of APP, tau, and receptors is critical.
Highly relevant at presynaptic terminals and endosomal compartments of excitatory neurons in hippocampus and neocortex, supporting neurotransmitter release and receptor recycling.
Early endosomes in neuronal soma and axons of projection neurons, especially in regions showing early endosomal enlargement in prodromal AD.
Key in synaptic junctions between neurons, at axon–glia interfaces in white matter, and in endothelial and pericyte junctions of the blood–brain barrier, all of which are compromised in AD.
Most relevant to cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons and associated glial cells in human brain regions where Aβ plaques form and mature into fibrillar aggregates.

Most relevant to neurons (especially cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons) and astrocytes/microglia, where extensive protein–protein interaction networks control synaptic signaling, APP processing, immune receptor signaling, and cytoskeletal organization that are disrupted in AD.
Predominantly neuronal (especially synapse-rich regions) but also active in astrocytes and microglia that handle misfolded protein clearance in AD cortex and hippocampus.
Active in neurons, astrocytes, and microglia within limbic and association cortices, where nuclear receptors regulate lipid metabolism, inflammatory tone, and neurotrophic responses.

pathway_name: Regulation of cholesterol biosynthesis by SREBP (SREBF)
cell_context_text: Most pertinent to neurons and astrocytes in brain regions with high synaptic density (hippocampus, frontal and temporal cortex), where cholesterol supply and turnover tightly control synaptic membrane composition.

Primarily pertinent to excitatory and inhibitory neurons with high tau expression in hippocampus and association cortex, where tau-binding partners in axons and dendrites regulate microtubule dynamics, axonal transport, and synaptic structure, and where neurofibrillary tangle formation is most prominent in AD.

Most relevant in neurons (particularly hippocampal and cortical pyramidal neurons) and astrocytes/oligodendrocytes, which experience high oxidative load, as well as microglia that generate ROS in inflammatory responses.

Critical across neurons (tau and synaptic receptor phosphorylation), microglia and astrocytes (inflammatory signaling cascades), and cerebrovascular cells, reflecting system-wide kinase/phosphatase signaling alterations in AD.
Most salient in neurons and glial cells in cortex and hippocampus, where long-term epigenetic changes reshape memory-related and inflammatory gene expression programs.

pathway_name: regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II
cell_context_text: Operative in essentially all brain cell types, with strongest disease impact in excitatory neurons and microglia where transcriptional reprogramming drives synaptic dysfunction and neuroinflammation.

Relevant in neuronal nuclei, where heterochromatin architecture influences genome stability and long-term repression/activation of stress and synaptic genes, and in microglia where chromatin states encode inflammatory memory.

Primarily active in microglia and astrocytes (LXR/PPAR-ApoE and lipid handling, inflammatory tone) and in certain neuronal populations (ESR1- and RAR-mediated survival and plasticity), as well as at the neurovascular unit for lipid transport and barrier function.

Especially critical in neurons of hippocampus and neocortex, where high proteostatic demand at synapses renders UCHL1/USP14/UBQLN1 function essential to prevent accumulation of tau and other aggregation-prone proteins.

Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons and their synaptic compartments, where E3 ligases regulate turnover of tau, synaptic receptors, and signaling proteins; glial cells (astrocytes and microglia) also contribute via ubiquitin ligases controlling inflammatory and clearance pathways in AD plaques and tangles.
Specifically maps to dendritic spines of glutamatergic neurons in hippocampus (CA1, dentate gyrus) and association cortex, where PSD reorganization and thinning are early AD features.

Pertains to the broader postsynaptic apparatus in forebrain excitatory neurons, including spines in medial temporal lobe and neocortex that exhibit early plasticity deficits and structural degeneration in AD.
Most relevant to excitatory synapses of hippocampal and cortical pyramidal neurons, whose loss closely tracks memory impairment in AD.

Most relevant to excitatory glutamatergic synapses in hippocampal and cortical pyramidal neurons, where neurexin–neuroligin and SynCAM-mediated adhesions maintain spine structure and where early synapse loss is a defining lesion in AD brains.

Most relevant to highly active cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons and possibly vulnerable excitatory neurons in association cortices, where intense protein synthesis and synaptic turnover place heavy demands on ER folding and ERAD. It may also extend to glial cells (astrocytes, microglia) engaged in inflammatory and secretory responses in AD, but the module’s synaptic focus points primarily to neuronal ER stress.

Most relevant in vulnerable cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons where RNA-binding proteins orchestrate local translation and stress responses; also in glia where RNA metabolism modulates inflammatory gene expression.
Most relevant to post-mitotic cortical and hippocampal neurons in AD, where nuclear integrity, DNA damage signaling, and transcription of synaptic and memory-related genes are disrupted.
Primarily nuclear/nucleolar in neurons and astrocytes, where snoRNPs regulate rRNA modifications that tune translational capacity under chronic AD-associated stress.
Nucleolar and nucleoplasmic compartments of neurons engaged in high translational demand, where rRNA-binding proteins mediate ribosome assembly and respond to nucleolar stress.

Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons, where high translational demand and documented nucleolar stress in AD brains would make impaired ribosome production particularly detrimental.
Similarly centered in neuronal nucleoli of vulnerable brain regions, linking to observed nucleolar fragmentation and reduced rRNA synthesis in AD.
Particularly pertinent to pyramidal neurons and other large projection neurons in AD cortex and hippocampus, which depend heavily on robust ribosome biogenesis and show early nucleolar stress.

pathway_name: rRNA processing in the nucleus and cytosol
cell_context_text: Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons, where nucleolar stress and ribosome loss are documented, but also in supporting glial cells that experience chronic inflammatory and oxidative stress in AD.

pathway_name: rRNA modification in the nucleus and cytosol
cell_context_text: Primarily pertinent to neurons with high translational demands at synapses, where altered rRNA modification patterns could selectively affect local protein synthesis and plasticity.

Broadly relevant to both neurons and glia in affected AD brain regions (e.g., hippocampus, entorhinal cortex), as global RNA metabolic defects can influence synaptic maintenance, glial reactivity, and cell stress responses across cell types.

Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons and other long-lived central neurons, where nucleolar integrity and sustained protein synthesis are essential and where AD pathology prominently develops.
Broadly relevant in neurons and glial cells in AD cortex and hippocampus, where widespread splicing and RNA maturation changes have been detected.

Applies to neuronal nuclei and perinuclear regions in affected brain regions, where RNP assembly and RNA metabolism shape synaptic gene expression and vulnerability to aggregation-prone RNA-binding proteins.
Encompasses neuronal and glial RNA metabolism in AD brain tissue, capturing system-wide transcriptome remodeling under chronic stress.
Most pertinent to nucleoli of excitatory neurons in AD-affected cortical and hippocampal regions, where subtle rRNA maturation defects can impact synaptic protein synthesis.

pathway_name: endonucleolytic cleavage of tricistronic rRNA transcript (SSU-rRNA, 5.8S rRNA, LSU-rRNA)
cell_context_text: Localized to neuronal nucleoli in grey matter regions with high vulnerability, such as entorhinal cortex and hippocampus.
Neuronal nucleoli in hippocampus and association cortex, where early pre-rRNA processing is critical and its perturbation has been linked to AD-related nucleolar pathology.
Most relevant in neuronal nucleoli and Cajal bodies in AD-vulnerable brain areas, where subtle changes in rRNA modification can have outsized effects on proteostasis.
Likely most impactful in neurons with high firing rates and metabolic demand, where altered ribosome function would quickly translate into synaptic dysfunction.
Applies to neurons and, potentially, astrocytes and microglia in AD cortex and hippocampus, where epitranscriptomic changes can reprogram stress and inflammatory responses.

Most pertinent in the same vulnerable neuronal populations (e.g., hippocampal CA1, entorhinal cortex) in which widespread transcriptional reprogramming and DNA-damage–linked transcriptional stress occur during AD progression.
Neuronal and glial nucleoli involved in large ribosomal subunit maturation, likely in regions with pronounced metabolic and translational burden such as hippocampus and frontal cortex.
Predominantly in neuronal nuclei and cytoplasm (including dendrites) where RNA methylation fine-tunes translation and RNA stability during synaptic activity and stress responses.
Localized to neuronal nuclei in cortex and hippocampus, where efficient snRNP/snoRNP biogenesis ensures proper splicing and noncoding RNA maturation of AD-relevant transcripts.
Centered in neuronal nuclei where spliceosome activity shapes isoform expression of APP, MAPT, and synaptic genes in AD-affected regions.
Broadly relevant in neurons and glia across AD-affected regions, reflecting combined roles in RNA and potentially protein or small-molecule methylation that shape epigenetic and translational states.
Most relevant to excitatory and inhibitory synapses in hippocampal and neocortical pyramidal neurons and interneurons, where synaptic loss and remodeling are hallmark AD features.
Broadly maps to CNS neurons, with strongest relevance in cortical and hippocampal circuits that subserve memory and cognition in AD.
Most relevant in excitatory presynaptic boutons of hippocampal CA1/CA3 pyramidal neurons and association cortex, where early synaptic loss is pronounced in AD.
Most relevant to cortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons where early synaptic loss and network hyper/hypoactivity occur in AD.
Pertinent to glutamatergic and GABAergic synapses in hippocampus and association cortex, and to a lesser extent subcortical nuclei affected in later AD stages.
Primarily axons and presynaptic terminals of hippocampal and cortical neurons, including long-range projection neurons vulnerable in AD.
Presynaptic boutons of glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons in hippocampus and association cortex.
Pertinent to axons and dendrites of cortical and hippocampal neurons undergoing degeneration, as well as cholinergic projections from basal forebrain.
Especially critical in neuronal and possibly microglial plasma membranes in gray matter regions rich in plaques and tangles, where receptor–Aβ interactions and signaling changes occur.
Relevant to immature or regenerating neurites in hippocampus and cortex, and to growth-cone–like structures during neuritic sprouting around plaques.
Localized to presynaptic terminals of glutamatergic neurons in hippocampus and neocortex, and to vulnerable cholinergic synapses.

Most relevant to dopaminergic neurons in midbrain regions (e.g., ventral tegmental area) and their projections to prefrontal cortex and limbic structures, which modulate motivation and executive function in AD.
Central to presynaptic terminals of hippocampal and cortical neurons, including Schaffer collateral and corticocortical synapses that underlie declarative memory.

Applies to both pre- and post-synaptic compartments across cortical and hippocampal excitatory synapses, where adhesion complex disruption is closely tied to dendritic spine loss and synaptic disconnection in AD.
Neuronal synaptic junctions and cerebrovascular endothelial tight/adherens junctions contributing to blood–brain barrier integrity.
Centered on hippocampal and cortical glutamatergic synapses that mediate memory and higher cognition, the principal sites of Aβ-induced synaptic toxicity.
Axons and presynaptic compartments of neurons forming cortical–hippocampal and cortico-cortical circuits.
Primarily at dendritic spines of pyramidal neurons in hippocampus and temporal/parietal cortex, where PSD disorganization and spine loss are well-documented in AD.
Neuron–neuron and neuron–glia junctions in cortical and hippocampal gray matter, including synaptic adhesion zones that maintain circuit integrity.
Neuronal and glial adhesion to extracellular matrix in gray matter and at neurovascular units, influencing synapse stability and immune cell interactions in AD.
Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons, where APP trafficking and receptor endocytosis drive Aβ generation and synaptic receptor remodeling.

Most relevant to cortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons, particularly presynaptic terminals where SNARE complexes mediate neurotransmitter release, but also to other brain cells where SNARE-dependent vesicle trafficking supports secretion and membrane turnover.
Pertinent to synaptic junctions between excitatory neurons and also neuron–glia contacts in hippocampus and association cortex vulnerable in AD.
Central at excitatory and inhibitory synapses in hippocampus and neocortex, where synapse loss strongly correlates with cognitive decline.
Most relevant to excitatory neurons in hippocampus and cortex, especially presynaptic terminals of glutamatergic pyramidal neurons that degenerate early in AD.
Most relevant in neuronal membranes of cortical and hippocampal neurons, including dendritic spines and axon terminals rich in APP and glutamate receptors.
Key in CA1–CA3 hippocampal circuits and cortical pyramidal neuron synapses mediating memory and cognition.
Applies broadly to neurons, with particular importance in long-projection cortical and hippocampal neurons where axonal autophagosome trafficking is crucial.
Relevant to both neurons and glial cells (astrocytes and microglia), reflecting global defects in proteostasis and organelle quality control in AD brains.

Primarily neuronal (synaptic receptor and APP internalization in pyramidal neurons) but also critical in microglia and astrocytes for uptake of Aβ and debris, and in endothelial cells of the blood–brain barrier regulating transcytosis.

Neurons in hippocampus and cortex are key, given their reliance on basal autophagy to clear long-lived proteins and organelles, but glial autophagy in microglia and astrocytes also shapes inflammatory responses and plaque-associated clearance.
Most relevant to excitatory and inhibitory neurons in hippocampus and cortex, where activity-dependent Ca2+ entry drives plasticity and is disrupted early in AD.
Focused on presynaptic terminals of cortical and hippocampal neurons where early release defects appear in AD.
Predominantly neuronal (axonal and dendritic trafficking), but also involves glial cells where vesicular trafficking supports neurotransmitter recycling and inflammatory signaling.
Enriched in presynaptic terminals and, more broadly, in neurons throughout vulnerable brain regions mediating synaptic vesicle exocytosis.
Most relevant in neuronal soma of hippocampal and cortical neurons where Golgi fragmentation and trafficking defects are observed.

Centered in neurons’ endosomal and synaptic vesicle compartments in vulnerable regions such as hippocampal CA1 and entorhinal cortex, but also present in glia affecting APP trafficking and Aβ clearance.

Predominantly presynaptic terminals of cortical and hippocampal neurons, where SNARE-dependent vesicle fusion is essential for maintaining synaptic strength and connectivity that are lost over AD progression.
Important in cortical and hippocampal interneurons and projection neurons that release neuropeptides and modulators influencing network excitability.
Relevant in neurons and glia (especially microglia and astrocytes) across AD-affected regions, where defective lysosomal clearance contributes to protein accumulation.
Prominent in dystrophic neurites and axons of hippocampal and cortical neurons where autophagic vacuoles accumulate in AD.

Although named for dopaminergic synapses, the validated signal most plausibly reflects conserved presynaptic machinery at cortical and hippocampal glutamatergic synapses, which are selectively vulnerable in AD and underpin episodic memory.
Especially pertinent to microglia (Aβ and debris clearance) and to neurons in the context of degradation of internalized material and damaged organelles.

Strongly linked to microglia in AD plaques as professional phagocytes clearing Aβ and synapses, and additionally to neurons where phagosome-like compartments participate in axonal and synaptic cargo degradation.
Focused on presynaptic terminals of hippocampal and cortical neurons, where fine-tuned transmitter release is essential for memory circuits.

This pathway applies broadly to excitatory and inhibitory synapses, but its strongest disease relevance here is in hippocampal and cortical pyramidal neurons, where early Aβ-driven synaptic weakening, altered release probability, and eventual synapse loss are central to AD progression.
Similarly concentrated in presynaptic boutons of cortical and hippocampal neurons, influencing short-term plasticity and activity patterns in networks vulnerable in AD.
Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal neurons and reactive astrocytes/microglia exposed to oxidative and inflammatory stress in AD brains.
Primarily relevant to secretory neurons in vulnerable regions (e.g., hippocampal pyramidal cells) where APP and synaptic protein processing are intensive.

Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons at synaptic junctions and neuron–glia interfaces, where adhesion molecules maintain synaptic contacts and structural integrity, and in vascular/endothelial cells contributing to blood–brain barrier alterations.

Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons where dendritic arbor degeneration and axonal transport defects are hallmark AD features, directly tying this compartment to cognitive decline.
Most impactful in excitatory pyramidal neurons and their dendritic spines, where Rho-family control of actin dynamics governs spine stability and plasticity.
Pertinent both to excitatory synaptic junctions between neurons and to endothelial–glial junctions at the blood–brain barrier, key sites of synapse loss and barrier breakdown in AD brains.

Most relevant to microglia and infiltrating myeloid cells in the AD brain, where NOD-like receptors and related inflammatory mediators sense Aβ and damaged cellular components and drive chronic neuroinflammation.
Particularly crucial in long-projection neurons (e.g., cortical–hippocampal neurons) that depend on efficient axonal autophagy to clear damaged cargo from synaptic terminals.

Predominantly relevant to neurons (especially in hippocampus and cortex) and astrocytes experiencing high secretory and metabolic load, where sustained ER stress from misfolded APP, Aβ, and tau contributes to synaptic dysfunction and cell death; it may also be important in secretory endothelial and glial cells that manage vascular and inflammatory stress.
Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons and vulnerable interneurons undergoing stress-induced death, with contributions from reactive glia.

Especially relevant to perisynaptic and perivascular adhesion sites in neurons, astrocytes, and endothelial cells in cortical and hippocampal regions, where altered ECM–cell interactions and mechanosensing can influence synaptic maintenance and microvascular stability in AD.
Prominent in surviving neurons and glial cells attempting to counteract pro-death signals in AD-affected regions.
Broadly engaged across neurons, astrocytes, and microglia in AD cortex and hippocampus, reflecting chronic proteotoxic and oxidative stress.
Most critical in neurons with high secretory and trafficking demands (e.g., excitatory cortical and hippocampal neurons) where APP processing and receptor trafficking occur.
Relevant during both development and adult circuit remodeling in hippocampus and association cortex, where misregulated guidance signaling can drive maladaptive pruning in AD.
Central to presynaptic and postsynaptic compartments of hippocampal and cortical neurons, and to microglial/astrocytic secretory/endocytic functions handling Aβ.
Associated with highly stressed neuronal populations at the margins of plaques and tangles where pro-death signaling predominates.

Primarily relevant in long-projection neurons (cortical pyramidal cells, hippocampal neurons) where axonal and dendritic microtubules are essential for cargo transport, and in their axons coursing through white-matter tracts, which are vulnerable to early transport deficits in AD.
Encompasses synapses across cortical–hippocampal networks and other memory-related circuits whose functional decline characterizes AD.
Relevant to both synaptic contacts among neurons and neurovascular unit components (endothelial cells, pericytes, astrocytic endfeet) that form the blood–brain barrier in AD.
Most relevant in neurons and their processes (axons, dendrites) where K63-linked ubiquitination directs endosomal sorting and autophagic clearance of synaptic proteins and aggregates in AD.
Active in cortical and hippocampal neurons as well as glial cells, where polyubiquitin-binding adaptors handle misfolded proteins and damaged organelles that accumulate in AD.
Most relevant in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons undergoing early synaptic loss and degeneration in AD.

pathway_name: positive regulation of apoptotic signaling pathway
